name: Niger
summary: Independent from France in 1960; a Sahel country with one of the world’s fastest-growing populations, rich in uranium.

location.value: West Africa, landlocked; about 1.27 million km².

terrain.value: Mostly Sahara; the Niger River in the south-west.

climate.value: Very hot and dry across the Sahara in the north, and the Sahel in the south, with a short rainy season.

resources.value: Uranium, oil, gold, livestock and farmland along the Niger River.

disasters.value: Recurrent droughts (1970s, 1984, 2010) and floods along the Niger River.

population.value: 28,814,878 (2026 estimate, infobox); the article’s body gives 25,252,722 for 2021.

urbanisation.value: Niamey is the capital and largest city; most people still live in villages.

disease.value: Malaria, malnutrition and meningitis are widespread among children.

migration.value: A route for migrants crossing the Sahara.

economicBase.value: Farming, herding and uranium mining (French-led mines at Arlit).

tradeRoutes.value: Goods move by road through Benin and Nigeria, since Niger is landlocked, and across the Sahara to Algeria and Libya.

wealth.value: One of the poorest countries in the world, despite uranium and oil.

moneyAndTax.value: The West African CFA franc, shared with neighbours and pegged to the euro.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

governmentType.value: A semi-presidential republic under a military junta (the National Council for the Safeguard of the Homeland).

keyRulers.value: Hamani Diori (first president, overthrown in 1974 by Seyni Kountché, who ruled until November 1987); Ibrahim Baré Maïnassara (1996 coup, assassinated 9 April 1999). Later and present leaders are not named here.

succession.value: Military coups in 1974, 2010 and 2023; the 2023 coup overthrew the elected president.

institutions.value: Weak institutions, with several coups since independence and a constitution suspended after the 2023 coup.

stability.value: Military coups in 1974, 2010 and 2023; Tuareg rebellions in the 1990s and from 2007.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

armyAndTech.value: A national army that fights insurgent groups in the Sahel and has seized power at times.

majorWars.value: Tuareg rebellions in 1990–1995 (peace deal April 1995) and 2007 (over by 2009). The jihadist insurgency is not covered in the part read.

territoryChange.value: The borders drawn by France have stayed the same since independence.

alliancesRivals.value: Turned from France toward Russia after 2023.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: Literacy is among the lowest in the world, though schooling is growing.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: Roads and the Niger River; there is no railway.

languageWriting.value: French is official; Hausa, Zarma-Songhay, Tamasheq and other languages are widely spoken.

artsArchitecture.value: Tuareg silver jewellery and leatherwork, and the mud-brick buildings of Agadez, a World Heritage city.

socialStructure.value: Hausa, Zarma-Songhay, Tuareg, Fula and Kanuri communities, with a very young population.

sharedIdentity.value: A national identity built on Islam, shared Sahel traditions and a mix of ethnic groups.

dailyLife.value: Most families farm millet and sorghum or herd animals; many live in mud-brick houses.

neighbours.value: Algeria, Libya, Chad, Nigeria, Benin, Burkina Faso, Mali.

ideasReligions.value: Islam, practised by about 99 percent of the people.

colonisation.value: A French colony: Military Territory of Niger created 1904, a distinct colony from 1922, independent 3 August 1960.

riseSignals.value: Independence from France declared on 3 August 1960; Hamani Diori became the first president.

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

outcome.value: Niger continues as an independent state.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
